catalog_quote: Daly 1978 p.98: "Pike and Oram (P & O) posit two tones, high and low, and one degree of stress. Stress is said to be contrastive on the ultimate syllable of stems but to be present always on the penultimate syllable and always absent on the antepenultimate syllable. A monosyllabic enclitic occurs both with and without stress depending on whether the preceding morpheme conditions its presence or not. ... Stress is said to occur on the first syllable of bisyllabic morphemes (the most common pattern) with monosyllabic morphemes being unstressed. In my view Diuxi Mixtec, like other Mixtec languages, has only one (grammatically predictable) stress to a word and that which P & O call contrastive stress should not be identified with the predictable stress. ... Non-predictable stress which P & O recognize ... should be recognized as a feature of tone. This feature, which can be called Modificat…
sweep_summary: Single sweep item: Pike & Oram 1976 (Phonetica), the primary first-hand description of Diuxi stress. Its body remains closed everywhere checked (Unpaywall closed, Karger live page PPV USD 45, SIL record 2767 links only to karger.com, archive.org has only the 1976 volume index, Karger first-page preview not archived); the abstract was re-read on the live SIL and Karger pages and matches the carried text verbatim. Nothing read contradicts the catalog: Daly 1978 p.98 (deciding source, open text) gives one grammatically predictable stress on the first syllable of the bisyllabic morpheme = stem penult, never antepenult; Hyman 2005 p.178 and Penner 2019 p.91 both report P&O 1976 (pp.321-22) as couplet-initial stress with an unpredictable second stem-final stress (on stems with reconstructed final *ʔ) that Daly reanalyzes as tone; Kuiper & Oram 1991 pp.186-187 (Oram is a P&O co-author; offprint fetched sources from Wayback, 234 pp, no text layer) restate the two analyses without a placement rule. The MORPHOLOGICAL coding stands. Acquisition priority: P&O 1976 body high (13 pages, purchase or ILL) to get the placement rule in the authors' own words; the 1977 6-page tone-orthography ms (SIL 56222, Cloudflare-blocked, not in Wayback) low. OpenAlex and Google Books APIs rate-limited; Internet Archive intermittently offline. Saved

new_statements.quote: Each word in Diuxi Mixtec has a stressed syllable which is marked by a long vowel. In addition to this stress, some words have a second stress. This second stress occurs only on the last syllable of the word and is marked by intensity and by allotones of both high and low tone. There is a contrast of high versus low tone, and there are allotones which occur in relation to the presence versus absence of word-final stress.
new_statements.citation: Pike, Eunice V. & Joy Oram. 1976. Stress and tone in the phonology of Diuxi Mixtec. Phonetica 33(5):321-333, abstract (read on the live SIL archive record and the live Karger page; identical to the 2018 Karger snapshot already carried)
new_statements.reading: First-hand: exactly one stressed (vowel-lengthened) syllable per word, plus, in some words, a lexically restricted second stress confined to the word-final syllable, cued by intensity and tonal allotones. The abstract itself does not locate the primary stress; the placement rule (stem penult = couplet-initial, never antepenult, enclitics outside the count) is known through Daly 1978 p.98 and Penner 2019 p.91 (citing P&O pp.321-322), both consistent with the catalog's MORPHOLOGICAL coding.

sources.citation: Kuiper, Albertha & Joy Oram. 1991. A syntactic sketch of Diuxi-Tilantongo Mixtec. In Bradley & Hollenbach (eds.), Studies in the syntax of Mixtecan languages 3 (SIL/UTA PL 105), 179-408; section 0.2 Phonology pp.186-187
sources.quote: Two analyses have been proposed for the tone system of this language, one by Pike and Oram (1976), and one by Daly (1978). In the Pike and Oram system, there are two levels of tone, high and low, and also a contrastive stress. In the Daly system, there are two tone features, [High] and [Modified], which define four tones in underlying forms. ... An acute accent is used for high tone, a macron for mid tone, a circumflex for a high downglide, and a vertical stroke for stress; low tone is unmarked.
sources.note: Oram (co-author of P&O 1976) restates the two analyses (H/L tone + contrastive stress vs. [High]/[Modified] four tones) and marks stress with a vertical stroke in both notations; no statement of where the predictable stress falls.

sources.quote: "In the Mixtec dialects/languages stems are generally disyllabic ('couplets'), with stress on their first syllable. Such stem-initial stress often conditions lengthening of the first vowel or second consonant. Certain dialects, however, have been claimed to have potentially two stresses per stem or word. According to E. Pike & Oram (1976), a second unpredictable stress occurs on the second syllable of some, but not all stems in Diuxi Mixtec—specifically on those for which a final *[glottal] has been reconstructed. ... the alleged stem-final stresses in Diuxi have been reanalyzed in terms of to
sources.note: Secondary report of P&O 1976: couplet-initial (stem-first-syllable) stress as in Mixtec generally, plus an unpredictable second stress on the stem-final syllable of stems with reconstructed final *ʔ; endorses Daly's tonal reanalysis of the second 'stress'.
